chunks.section: Maximizing Capacity Utilization of LoRA Adapters for Mitigating the Learning-Forgetting Trade-off
chunks.text: Tomohiro Sawada † † thanks: Corresponding author: tsawada@gatech.edu . Affiliation: School of Interactive Computing Kartik Goyal Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA; Hu et al., 2022 ) is a standard parameter-efficient alternative to full fine-tuning: it scales to large models, is easy to compose with existing training stacks, and is widely treated as the default way to specialize a pretrained language model on a new task or domain Schulman and Thinking Machines Lab (2025) ; Biderman et al. (2024) . A common piece of practitioner wisdom is that increasing LoRA rank increases adapter capacity: a larger r r enlarges the low-rank update subspace and can support richer task-specific changes Raschka (2023) ; Schulman and Thinking Machines Lab (2025) ; Liu et al. (2024b) . This intuition is appealing and often borne out at moderate ranks, yet it rests on an implicit assumption that is rarely checked: that the adapter actually uses the subspace it is given.

In parallel, fine-tuning, whether full-rank or parameter-efficient, faces a persistent learning–forgetting tension. Fitting a target distribution can improve task metrics while erasing competence on broad pretraining domains, and heterogeneous or sequential training regimes exacerbate the trade-off Kirkpatrick et al. (2017) ; Hu et al. (2022) . LoRA is not exempt: in mixed-domain and continual-learning settings, adapters often lag full fine-tuning on target-task fit while still paying a substantial retention cost on pretraining proxies Biderman et al. (2024) ; Shuttleworth et al. (2024) . Prior work has proposed many remedies, such as stronger parameterizations Kopiczko et al. (2024) , norm constraints Wang et al. (2025) , spectral initialization Meng et al. (2025) , and deliberately tiny adapters Morris et al. (2026) . However, these approaches frequently reallocate the trade-off rather than improve it: methods that fit the fine-tuning mixture well can forget aggressively, whereas methods that limit forgetting often underfit the new data (Figure 2 ).

We argue that a useful missing variable in this picture is not nominal configured rank r r but the actual realized adapter capacity that we measure in terms of effective rank . Let Δ ​ W \Delta W denote the accumulated LoRA update on a target layer. Following Roy and Vetterli (2007) , we measure how many directions effectively carry singular-value mass using the effective rank erank ⁡ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}(\Delta W) , a continuous relaxation of matrix rank obtained from the entropy of the normalized spectrum. Intuitively, erank ⁡ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}(\Delta W) reports how uniformly the update distributes its singular-value mass across its singular directions: a highly skewed spectrum behaves like a low-rank update in practice even when r r is large. Across three fine-tuning settings, standard LoRA training underutilizes capacity in exactly this sense: we observe in Figure 1 that the utilization quotient erank ⁡ ( Δ ​ W ) / r \mathrm{erank}(\Delta W)/r tends to be much smaller than 1.0 1.0 and even more strikingly, it falls as configured rank grows (Section 2 ). The key observation is therefore that configured rank is an unreliable proxy for usable capacity : scaling r r alone does not reliably deliver “more adapter” in the sense that matters for learning and retention.

This distinction matters because the learning–forgetting trade-off is not only about how large an update is, but about how that update is distributed across the orthogonal directions of the weight. Spectral analyses of finetuned weights in prior work emphasize that adaptation can introduce directions weakly aligned with the pretrained spectrum (so-called intruder dimensions ), and that the prevalence and weighting of such directions correlate with forgetting Shuttleworth et al. (2024) . However, in our analysis (§ 5 ), every method that fits the mixture well, dense fine-tuning included, places most of its singular-value mass on such directions; only the methods that underfit (VeRA, TinyLoRA, SVF) avoid them. Therefore, we argue that the relevant question is not whether intruder dimensions exist, but whether the dominant part of the update uses the allocated rank budget in a balanced, information-bearing way. We therefore ask: can we improve the learning–forgetting frontier by maximizing realized capacity during training? Since erank ⁡ ( Δ ​ W ) ≤ r \mathrm{erank}(\Delta W)\leq r Roy and Vetterli (2007) , increasing utilization means driving the normalized spectrum toward uniformity subject to the task loss.

Concretely, we study regularized training objectives that augment the standard language-modeling loss L L with a capacity regularization term that focuses on maximizing the effective rank. Direct spectral differentiation requires care at rank-deficient updates and incurs SVD overhead (Appendix D .1). We therefore use an SVD-free surrogate, the Rényi-2 effective rank erank 2 ​ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}_{2}(\Delta W) . We develop two approaches to increasing this effective-rank surrogate. First, norm-bounded capacity maximization couples a Roy–Vetterli lower bound with Norm-Bounded LoRA (NB-LoRA) Wang et al. (2025) : by enforcing an operator-norm cap and maximizing the Frobenius norm within that cap, one can raise effective rank through a principled constrained reparameterization. This strategy works in practice but limits the adapter weight updates to a specialized parameterization which often results in unstable training empirically. Therefore, we propose a simpler, differentiable, parameterization-agnostic and easy-to-optimize regularization strategy called the Rényi-2 penalty as our main method, which directly maximizes erank 2 ​ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}_{2}(\Delta W) . This penalty is not only applicable to vanilla LoRA, but also to improved spectral variants such as PiSSA Meng et al. (2025) and LoRA-XS Bałazy et al. (2025) .

We evaluate whether higher realized rank shifts the learning–forgetting frontier across settings that stress different aspects of adaptation. In mixed-domain fine-tuning, at λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 , the penalty lowers mean Wiki perplexity relative to unpenalized LoRA at every tested rank of at least 16 16 on Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. Training perplexity is generally similar or improved, with a larger increase for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct at r = 16 r=16 (Section 4.4 ).

Increasing λ \lambda raises the reported effective rank. At the maximal rank on Qwen2.5-0.5B (Figure 2 ), λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 and 0.1 0.1 improve both mixture fit and retention, whereas the single run at λ = 1 \lambda=1 improves retention with Train PPL within standard LoRA’s run-to-run variation. PiSSA and LoRA-XS Meng et al. (2025) ; Bałazy et al. (2025) have the highest Wiki perplexities, despite lower reported mean StarCoder and GSM8K perplexities than standard LoRA; VeRA, SVF, and TinyLoRA Kopiczko et al. (2024) ; Sun et al. (2022) ; Morris et al. (2026) limit forgetting primarily by underfitting the mixture. Applied to PiSSA and LoRA-XS, the regularizer can improve both task fit and retention. The same pattern holds on single-task fine-tuning setups like GSM8K, where our method, especially with late-start schedules, improves target-task fit while reducing forgetting on the reference probes. Our singular-direction analysis (§ 5 ) shows what the penalty leaves unchanged: penalized and standard LoRA place a similar share of singular-value mass on directions with no strong counterpart in the pretrained basis (0.97 vs. 0.96), yet the penalized adapters forget far less.

In summary, our core contributions are: i) we identify systematic capacity underutilization in standard LoRA training, especially at high configured rank, and argue that realized effective rank, not nominal rank, is the relevant unit of analysis for adapter capacity, ii) we formulate effective-rank maximization as a principled objective atop standard language-modeling loss, with both a norm-bounded reparameterization route (NB-LoRA) and a parameterization-agnostic surrogate, iii) we introduce the Rényi-2 penalty , a unitary-invariant, SVD-free effective-rank regularizer that is simple to implement and stable to optimize, and demonstrate improvements in the learning–forgetting trade-off across mixed-domain and single-task fine-tuning settings, and iv) we provide spectral diagnostics (intruder mass, soft global coupling) that provide a novel lens to characterize the relationship between singular directions of updated weights and the pretrained weights.

chunks.section: Comparison to standard LoRA and dense down-projection fine-tuning.
chunks.text: Standard LoRA attains Train PPL 4.77 4.77 but underutilizes capacity ( erank = 361 \mathrm{erank}=361 in panel A). The dense down-projection fine-tuning baseline (a single run) has weaker mixture fit (Train PPL 5.64 5.64 ) but lower StarCoder and GSM8K perplexities ( 3.64 3.64 and 1.817 1.817 , versus 5.82 5.82 and 1.929 1.929 for standard LoRA). chunks.section: Methods that learn the mixture but forget pretraining.

chunks.section: Methods that limit forgetting by underfitting the mixture.
chunks.text: At the other extreme, VeRA Kopiczko et al. (2024) , SVF Sun et al. (2022) , and TinyLoRA keep Wiki and StarCoder perplexity low ( 13.0 13.0 – 13.2 13.2 and 3.8 3.8 – 3.9 3.9 ), but at the cost of weak mixture learning: Train PPL remains 9.7 9.7 – 11.5 11.5 . chunks.section: Rényi-2 penalty improves the learning–forgetting trade-off.

chunks.section: Norm-bounded LoRA recovers much of the gain.

chunks.section: 4.4 Effect of Rényi-2 penalty across LoRA rank configurations
chunks.text: Our main mixed-domain comparison uses the maximal matrix rank r = 896 r{=}896 for the adapted projections. We now examine smaller rank budgets ( r ∈ { 4 , 16 , 128 , 256 , 512 } r\in\{4,16,128,256,512\} ) to distinguish the effect of nominal rank from spectral utilization. Figure 3 summarizes this on Qwen2.5-0.5B with assistant-only SFT on the mixed-domain continual-learning proxy setting (run means; full metrics in Appendix Table 9 ).

chunks.section: Cross-model retention gains at a small penalty weight.
chunks.text: Across the reported mixed-domain rank sweeps on Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity relative to unpenalized LoRA at every tested rank of at least 16 16 (Tables 9 , 10 , and 11 ). Mean Train PPL improves or increases by at most 0.020 0.020 in all but one of these comparisons; the exception is Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct at r = 16 r=16 , where it increases from 4.211 4.211 to 4.524 4.524 . These results support a consistent Wiki retention benefit in this setting, but not universal improvement on both objectives.

The mixed-domain experiments above apply the penalty from the first step. Here we ask what the start step changes, using a short single-task run in which the early phase is a large share of training. Table 3 reports a scheduling ablation on SFT of Qwen2.5-0.5B on the Aya Hausa instruction-following dataset for ∼ 500 {\sim}500 optimizer steps ( ∼ 3 × 10 5 {\sim}3\times 10^{5} tokens). We fix the terminal penalty weight to λ 1 = 0.1 \lambda_{1}{=}0.1 and a linear ramp of length W = 200 W{=}200 steps, and vary the start step S S at which the Rényi-2 penalty is first applied to the language-modeling loss.

chunks.section: Retention improves whenever the penalty is used.
chunks.text: Across all choices of S S , adding the penalty reduces forgetting on the pretraining proxies: StarCoder and Wiki perplexity are lower than for standard LoRA ( 4.05 4.05 and 21.8 21.8 ) in every penalized row. The strongest retention is at early starts (e.g., S = 50 S{=}50 : StarCoder 3.75 3.75 , Wiki 18.7 18.7 ), while S = 400 S{=}400 still improves over standard LoRA ( 3.86 3.86 and 19.8 19.8 ) despite engaging the penalty only in the final segment of training.

In contrast, Train PPL worsens as the penalty is applied earlier: 22.6 22.6 (no penalty) → \rightarrow 24.7 24.7 at S = 0 S{=}0 , with intermediate values at S = 50 S{=}50 and S = 100 S{=}100 ( 23.9 23.9 and 23.7 23.7 ). Only a late start ( S = 400 S{=}400 ) recovers baseline-level Train PPL ( 22.4 22.4 ). The same trend appears in erank ⁡ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}(\Delta W) : early starts yield effective ranks of approximately 785 785 – 838 838 , whereas S = 400 S{=}400 yields erank = 430 \mathrm{erank}=430 , only modestly above unpenalized LoRA ( 341 341 ). On this short budget, S = 400 S{=}400 also does not complete the ramp, so the run ends with effective weight ≈ 0.05 {\approx}0.05 —yet retention still improves.

Two mechanisms may help explain the training–retention trade-off. First, linear mode connectivity ( Frankle et al., 2020 ) : after a sufficient number of steps, the model may enter a basin of the language-modeling loss in which the solution is comparatively robust to perturbations. Applying the penalty in that late phase reshapes the adapter spectrum without derailing Hausa fit. Activating it from the outset interferes with the initial trajectory into that basin and inflates Train PPL even when forgetting is minimized. Second, there is a more direct, penalty-specific effect. Start time is a second knob alongside λ \lambda : an early start maximizes retention and a late start protects fit. Three qualitative regimes emerge. First, VeRA and TinyLoRA exhibit near-saturated coupling to the pretrained spectrum: weighted unaligned mass is near zero, and the unaligned count is also small (especially for VeRA), with small H soft H_{\mathrm{soft}} . Second, a broad LoRA-like band—including Standard LoRA, Rényi-2 penalty, PiSSA, LoRA-XS, and (to a slightly lesser extent) dense down-projection fine-tuning—leaves ≳ 96 % \gtrsim 96\% of directions unaligned at this strict threshold. In this regime, count-based comparisons are nearly flat, but where the spectral mass lands still differs: LoRA-XS places the largest fraction of spectral weight on directions without a strong pretrained partner, consistent with its adaptation being carried by dominant singular directions that are more decoupled from pretraining. Third, SVF with an intermediate H soft H_{\mathrm{soft}} illustrates that count and mass can decouple sharply: it has near-zero weighted unaligned mass but a much lower unaligned rate than the LoRA-like band, indicating that SVF concentrates most of the finetuned matrix’s singular-value mass on a small set of strongly pretrained-like directions while leaving a long tail of low-weight directions without strong partners. In these experiments, fine-tuning produces many directions without a strong match to the pretrained singular basis; methods differ in how much singular-value mass these directions carry.

Roy and Vetterli (2007) ’s effective rank summarizes how uniformly singular-value mass is distributed; we build on their definition and on Rényi entropies Rényi (1961) ; Cover and Thomas (2006) to obtain a unitary-invariant surrogate ( erank 2 \mathrm{erank}_{2} ) suitable for gradient-based training. To our knowledge, prior PEFT work has not targeted maximizing realized adapter rank during language-model fine-tuning as a means to improve the learning–forgetting frontier; rank-stabilized scaling Kalajdzievski (2023) and spectral initializations Meng et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2024) address adjacent but distinct failure modes.

A large body of prior work studies how to configure LoRA—rank and scaling Raschka (2023) ; Kalajdzievski (2023) , which modules to target Schulman and Thinking Machines Lab (2025) , and whether LoRA can match full fine-tuning in post-training regimes Schulman and Thinking Machines Lab (2025) ; Biderman et al. (2024) . These works largely treat configured rank r r or trainable parameter count as mere hyperparameters. Orthogonal to utilization, PEFT methods also differ in their trainable budget and in how the update is tied to the pretrained spectrum. VeRA Kopiczko et al. (2024) , Singular Value fine-tuning Sun et al. (2022) , and TinyLoRA Morris et al. (2026) restrict trainable degrees of freedom by several orders of magnitude. LoRA-XS Bałazy et al. (2025) also reduces the budget, training only an r × r r\times r core inside a frozen truncated-SVD subspace ( 1.9 × 10 7 1.9\times 10^{7} versus 1.2 × 10 8 1.2\times 10^{8} parameters at r = 896 r{=}896 in our setup), yet still admits a rank- r r update. PiSSA Meng et al. (2025) keeps LoRA’s budget and instead changes the initialization to the principal singular directions of the pretrained weight. We benchmark against all three regimes in Section 4.1 ; our penalty is complementary in that it improves utilization within a fixed parameterization rather than reallocating the budget itself.

Fine-tuning improves target-task metrics but can erase competence on broad pretraining domains, and heterogeneous or sequential training amplifies the tension Kirkpatrick et al. (2017) . Biderman et al. (2024) systematically compare LoRA and full fine-tuning, showing that low-rank adapters typically learn less on the target domain but also forget less off it, and that full fine-tuning’s effective update rank can exceed typical LoRA configurations by an order of magnitude. Norm- and magnitude-aware variants such as DoRA Liu et al. (2024a) , DeLoRA Bini et al. (2025) , and Norm-Bounded LoRA Wang et al. (2025) pursue a related goal—making directional updates behave more like full fine-tuning Aghajanyan et al. (2020) —but through reparameterization rather than explicit control of spectral utilization. Continued-pretraining methods such as ReLoRA Lialin et al. (2023) accumulate high-rank structure by merging and restarting low-rank updates over long horizons; we instead ask how to use a single adapter’s rank budget more fully during standard SFT. A growing line of work engineers fine-tuning through the singular structure of weight matrices. PiSSA Meng et al. (2025) initializes adapters from dominant singular components; MiLoRA Wang et al. (2024) instead adapts minor components to reduce interference with pretrained knowledge; AdaLoRA Zhang et al. (2023) adaptively reallocates rank across modules; and SVF Sun et al. (2022) trains singular values directly. These methods change which subspace or spectrum is updated, often at the cost of an explicit or implicit SVD. Our Rényi-2 penalty is orthogonal and complementary to these approaches.

Standard LoRA training often underutilizes its allocated subspace so nominal rank is an unreliable proxy for usable adapter capacity in the learning–forgetting trade-off. We proposed effective-rank maximization via the Rényi-2 penalty, a parameterization-agnostic, SVD-free term added to the language-modeling loss, and showed across mixed-domain SFT, task-specific SFT, rank sweeps, and scheduling ablations that it can reduce forgetting on pretraining proxies while maintaining competitive target-task fit. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models, λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA, with mean Train PPL improving or increasing by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one comparison. Our single-task and scheduling experiments also demonstrate configuration-dependent learning and retention outcomes: the penalty can improve retention without a large training-fit cost, but does not eliminate the learning–forgetting trade-off. Spectral diagnostics provide descriptive comparisons of the resulting updates. Effective rank is therefore not merely a post-hoc diagnostic but a trainable objective that regularizes toward fuller utilization.

While capacity maximization improves the learning–forgetting frontier in several configurations, benefits depend on the metric and execution, and the method still requires task-specific tuning of λ \lambda and may not be beneficial when the goal is deliberate underfitting or strong retention of a very narrow domain. The present study focuses on LoRA-style adapters and closely related spectral variants; extending the same objective to other PEFT families or to full fine-tuning may require different regularization schedules or parameterizations.

The paper studies general-purpose language-model adaptation on public benchmark data and does not introduce new user data collection. The main ethical risk is indirect: methods that improve adaptation efficiency can be repurposed to more rapidly specialize models for harmful or deceptive uses. We therefore frame the contribution as an optimization and analysis tool, not as a deployment recommendation, and recommend the usual safeguards for downstream release, including dataset provenance checks, benchmark leakage review, and task-appropriate human oversight.

chunks.section: Rank one has no spectral utilization margin.
chunks.text: For a nonzero rank-one update, there is one nonzero singular value, so both normalized spectra have a single entry equal to 1 1 . Consequently, erank ⁡ ( Δ ​ W ) = erank 2 ​ ( Δ ​ W ) = 1 \mathrm{erank}(\Delta W)=\mathrm{erank}_{2}(\Delta W)=1 , independently of its magnitude and direction. The exact capacity term is therefore constant over nonzero rank-one updates and supplies no preference among them. This is an algebraic boundary case; we report no rank-one experiment. Numerical stabilization near the zero update is separate from this statement about the exact objective.

chunks.section: Small ranks limit the available benefit.
chunks.text: Table 9 illustrates the smallest measured mixed-domain rank, r = 4 r{=}4 . With λ = 0.1 \lambda{=}0.1 , the reported mean erank \mathrm{erank} increases from 3.014 3.014 to 4.000 4.000 , while mean Wiki PPL changes from 13.615 13.615 to 13.564 13.564 and mean StarCoder PPL from 3.926 3.926 to 3.942 3.942 ; mean Train PPL increases from 6.096 6.096 to 6.595 6.595 . Thus saturating the spectral rank can accompany only small, mixed changes in retention and worse training fit. The penalty redistributes energy among at most r r nonzero singular directions; it cannot increase the configured rank budget.

chunks.section: Maximal matrix rank still permits spectral concentration.
chunks.text: For an adapted matrix of shape d out × d in d_{\mathrm{out}}\times d_{\mathrm{in}} , the rank ceiling is min ⁡ { r , d out , d in } \min\{r,d_{\mathrm{out}},d_{\mathrm{in}}\} . The r = 896 r{=}896 mixed-domain comparison reaches the maximal matrix rank for the targeted Qwen2.5-0.5B projections, but standard LoRA realizes a mean effective rank of 360.537 360.537 . In Table 5 , λ = 0.1 \lambda{=}0.1 raises the mean to 887.772 887.772 , lowers mean Wiki PPL from 19.601 19.601 to 14.648 14.648 and mean StarCoder PPL from 5.815 5.815 to 4.098 4.098 , and improves mean Train PPL from 4.773 4.773 to 4.525 4.525 . These are comparisons within the rank- 896 896 setting; together with the smaller-rank sweep, they show that the scope for improving spectral utilization depends on the rank budget. At maximal rank, LoRA can represent any update to each targeted matrix, but its factorized optimization differs from optimizing that matrix directly. The factors contain r ⁡ ( d in + d out ) r(d_{\mathrm{in}}+d_{\mathrm{out}}) parameters per matrix, compared with d in ​ d out d_{\mathrm{in}}d_{\mathrm{out}} for a dense update; at maximal matrix rank the factor count exceeds the dense count. This regime tests spectral utilization without providing parameter savings for those matrices. Increasing r r beyond the matrix-rank ceiling does not expand the space of representable updates.

chunks.section: Maximum effective rank is not a performance optimum.
chunks.text: At r = 256 r{=}256 , increasing λ \lambda from 0.01 0.01 to 0.1 0.1 raises the reported mean erank \mathrm{erank} from 250.540 250.540 to 255.777 255.777 , but mean Train PPL worsens from 4.465 4.465 to 4.559 4.559 , even as mean Wiki PPL improves from 14.145 14.145 to 13.975 13.975 (Table 9 ). Effective rank describes spectral utilization, while the task loss and retention probes determine whether that utilization is useful. Penalty strength must therefore be chosen for the desired learning–retention balance.

chunks.text: This appendix describes implementation details for the subspace alignment metrics used in our analysis. The main goal is to compute alignment between a source singular-vector basis and a target top- k k subspace efficiently and reproducibly.

Let V s , V t ∈ ℝ d × d V_{s},V_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} contain the right singular vectors of the source and target update matrices, respectively. For Tables 29 – 31 , each update is defined as Δ ​ W = W ft − W 0 \Delta W=W_{\mathrm{ft}}-W_{0} . For example, the source may be a Rényi-2-penalized LoRA solution and the target may be a dense down-projection fine-tuning solution or a standard LoRA solution. We are interested in comparing subspaces spanned by selected sets of k k columns of V s V_{s} to the target top- k k subspace 𝒮 t ( k ) := span ⁡ { v t , 1 , … , v t , k } . \mathcal{S}_{t}^{(k)}:=\operatorname{span}\{v_{t,1},\dots,v_{t,k}\}. (21) Let Q t := [ v t , 1 , … , v t , k ] ∈ ℝ d × k Q_{t}:=[v_{t,1},\ldots,v_{t,k}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} (22) be an orthonormal basis for this target subspace. For a subset R ⊆ { 1 , … , d } R\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\} of size k k , let Q s , R := [ v s , i ] i ∈ R ∈ ℝ d × k Q_{s,R}:=[v_{s,i}]_{i\in R}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} (23) be an orthonormal basis for the corresponding source subspace. chunks.section: I.2 Precomputing Per-Direction Target Overlap Scores
